                     REPLY BRIEF OF COLONIAL PIPELINE COMPANY
                         REGARDING MONETARY SANCTIONS

TO:    The Honorable Jeremy Hessler
       Presiding Administrative Law Judge

       Pursuant to the July 17, 2026 Order Directing Briefing and Status Reports issued in the

captioned proceeding (“July 17 Order”), Colonial Pipeline Company (“Colonial”) hereby submits

this Reply Brief on the issue of monetary sanctions. This Reply Brief responds to the Initial Brief

of Atlantic Trading & Marketing, Inc. (“ATMI”) that was filed in the captioned proceeding on

August 20, 2026 (“ATMI Initial Brief”).

       Summary.       ATMI’s Initial Brief is fundamentally flawed, as it fails to address the

subsequent developments the Presiding Judge directed the parties to discuss and instead relies on




                                                1
                                        PUBLIC VERSION
                              CUI//PRIV/HC MATERIAL REMOVED



a narrative riddled with mischaracterizations and factual inaccuracies.                  Further, the record

demonstrates that Colonial acted in good faith in the settlement process, with ATMI’s opening

request for a settlement payment from Colonial that was [BEGIN CUI//PRIV/HC]

[END CUI//PRIV/HC] recommended by the Presiding Judge in the May 2026 Order 1 nearly

collapsing settlement discussions before they even meaningfully began. More importantly, the

ATMI Initial Brief makes clear that ATMI had the Powder Springs Logistics, LLC (“PSL”)

information and data that it needed to perform the corroborative analysis that it sought to include

in its rebuttal testimony, and it received all of that PSL-related data from Colonial months prior to

ATMI’s rebuttal testimony deadline. ATMI has suffered no prejudice, much less undue prejudice.

In fact, ATMI never even sought the imposition of monetary sanctions against Colonial in the first

place, but rather sought certain evidentiary rulings and adverse inferences that it did not receive. 2

The Presiding Judge should reject ATMI’s arguments, recognize the gamesmanship for what it is,

and decline to impose sanctions on Colonial in the forthcoming Initial Decision.

I.      Introduction

        In the July 17 Order, the Presiding Judge permitted the parties in this proceeding to submit

initial and reply briefs to “address any materials, information, and subsequent developments

relevant to the Commission’s resolution of the recommended sanctions.” 3                      Separately, the

Presiding Judge encouraged the parties to settle this issue, with the Presiding Judge stating that he

would consider “the efforts of both parties to settle this issue” and explain the relevancy of that

effort, or lack of effort, to the Commission in his initial decision. 4

  Atlantic Trading & Marketing, Inc.’s Motion for Sanctions in the Form of Evidentiary Rulings, Docket Nos. OR22-
5-001 et al., at 2 (filed Feb. 18, 2026) (“ATMI Motion for Sanctions”).
3
  July 17 Order at P 3 (emphasis added).

                                                       2
                                          PUBLIC VERSION
                                CUI//PRIV/HC MATERIAL REMOVED



         Although the ATMI Initial Brief purports to address “facts and developments relevant to

the Commission’s resolution” of the monetary sanctions issue in accordance with Paragraph 3 of

the July 17 Order, 5 it does not. Instead, the ATMI Initial Brief almost exclusively (1) repeats

conclusions reached by the Presiding Judge in prior orders, and (2) discusses the efforts of Colonial

and ATMI to settle this issue, with ATMI attempting to portray Colonial’s actions during those

settlement discussions as not in good faith. As explained below, ATMI’s characterization of

Colonial’s settlement efforts is wrong, and the parties’ efforts to settle this issue, while ultimately

fruitless, cannot be used as evidence to resolve the merits of this dispute. As such, most of the

ATMI Initial Brief should be rejected as irrelevant to the Commission’s resolution of this issue.

By contrast, in accordance with Paragraph 3 of the July 17 Order, the Colonial Initial Brief 6

discusses those subsequent developments that conclusively prove what Colonial has maintained

from the beginning: that ATMI has suffered no “undue” prejudice as a result of Colonial’s actions,

and, as such, no sanctions should be imposed on Colonial. 7

         In addition to reciting the Presiding Judge’s previous findings, ATMI further argues that,

based on those prior orders, the Presiding Judge should reconsider imposing an even higher

monetary sanction—$567,530—against Colonial given the degree of Colonial’s purported

“misconduct” and “misrepresentations.” 8 However, ATMI omits key undisputed facts from its

argument.      For example, ATMI refers to the May 2026 Order’s finding that Colonial had

“repeatedly misrepresented” to ATMI that the PSL governing agreements did not give Colonial

the “right to obtain basic financial information concerning Powder Springs” and/or “were ‘silent

as to this issue.’” 9 Yet ATMI knows full well that this is not a factually accurate recitation; at the

time of those alleged representations, Colonial had already provided not only “basic financial

information” but also detailed financial information regarding all aspects of PSL’s operations,

including Profit & Loss (“P&L”) statements that ATMI acknowledges contained all of the

information necessary for ATMI’s witness Mr. Hollerbach to perform the corroborative analysis

that he was seeking to perform. 10 Indeed, while the “silent as to this issue” email communication

has been unfortunately (and inaccurately) construed as a representation by Colonial that it was

unable to obtain and produce any PSL-related data, that very same email communication makes

clear that Colonial had already produced to ATMI all of the material that was in Colonial’s

possession, custody and control, which is information that Colonial had obtained from ONEOK

(the other member and operator of PSL) in the normal course of business in accordance with the

PSL governing agreements. 11 Furthermore, that now-controversial email was in response to an

informal request by ATMI’s counsel that Colonial produce the PSL governing agreements outside

of the normal discovery process, not a formal discovery request; when ATMI actually requested

the PSL formation documents in a discovery request, Colonial produced them.

        Despite ATMI’s attempt to portray Colonial’s alleged “misrepresentations” as established

fact, Colonial continues to maintain that it and its counsel have engaged in no wrongdoing. The

entirety of this issue, including the Presiding Judge’s recommendation of monetary sanctions,

hinges on ATMI’s interpretation of a Delaware statue regarding the information that one member

of a joint venture can obtain from another member, as applied to the PSL governing agreements. 12

However, as Colonial has previously explained, there is a significant body of caselaw interpreting

that same Delaware statute that fully supports Colonial’s position—i.e., just because Colonial has

an ownership interest in PSL does not mean that it is automatically entitled to seek and obtain

every document or piece of data that is maintained by the other member (and operator) of PSL.13

Moreover, regardless of the correct interpretation of the Delaware statute, it is undisputed that

Colonial produced all of the responsive PSL information and data within its possession and did

not physically possess or have access to the limited additional PSL information that ATMI sought;

Colonial’s only option to obtain those materials was to take legal action against its joint venture

partner, which is the same option available to ATMI.

        Stripping away all of ATMI’s rhetoric attempting to portray Colonial as a bad actor, the

facts prove the contrary. ATMI fully admits in the ATMI Initial Brief that Mr. Hollerbach was

able to perform the “corroborative” analysis that he sought to perform, using the PSL data that

ATMI requested from Colonial and which Colonial produced back in June-August 2025. 14 The

record shows that Mr. Hollerbach’s “corroborative” analysis was first presented in his rebuttal

testimony that was filed in November 2025 and was based solely on information produced by

Colonial. 15 Mr. Hollerbach confirmed the accuracy of that analysis in his supplemental rebuttal

testimony, even acknowledging that most of the information that ONEOK later produced in April

2026 was the same as the material that Colonial had produced nearly 10 months prior, in June

2025. 16 Although ATMI alleges that it did not receive all of the PSL information it requested

(which, notably, ATMI fails to describe in any detail in the ATMI Initial Brief), Mr. Hollerbach’s

testimony indicates that ATMI did not even request the “missing” material (specifically, butane

and transportation invoices) from Colonial in the data requests that initiated this dispute. 17 Despite

numerous rounds of briefing and pleadings on this issue, ATMI has never contested these facts,

yet continues to claim that it suffered “undue” prejudice as a result of Colonial’s actions. The facts

simply do not support this claim.

II.     Argument

        A.       The ATMI Initial Brief confirms ATMI did not suffer “undue” prejudice from
                 Colonial’s actions.

        As noted, the majority of the ATMI Initial Brief focuses on the settlement negotiations

between Colonial and ATMI, which, as Colonial explains below, cannot be considered in the

Commission’s resolution of this issue on the merits. A single paragraph in the ATMI Initial Brief

(on page 12) discusses “[o]ther developments occurring after the [May 2026 Order]” that ATMI

claims “support an award of the full amount of fees incurred by ATMI.” 18 There, ATMI refers to

Mr. Hollerbach’s supplemental rebuttal testimony, where he testified that “ATMI still ha[d] not

received all of the Powder Springs information.” 19 ATMI then theorizes that “it is not known what

other information not produced would have further corroborated ATMI’s evidence.” 20

        ATMI’s speculation that there may have been “other” information it could have reviewed

and potentially used to perform further “corroborative” calculations does not support a finding that

ATMI suffered “undue prejudice,” particularly given that ATMI confirms “Mr. Hollerbach was

able to present testimony corroborating ATMI’s blend margins with those earned by Powder


17
   Colonial Initial Brief at 8-9.
18
   ATMI Initial Brief at 12.
19
   This is the same statement referenced in the May 2026 Order to demonstrate the alleged “undue” prejudice suffered
by ATMI. May 2026 Order at P 25.
20
   ATMI Initial Brief at 12.


                                                         6
                                                 PUBLIC VERSION
                                       CUI//PRIV/HC MATERIAL REMOVED



Springs based on the information provided.” 21 While ATMI is deliberately vague in its statement

about the “information provided” that it used to perform the “corroborative” calculations, the

record shows that this “information” is the very data that Colonial produced to ATMI months

before ATMI’s rebuttal testimony deadline. 22 Recognition of this point—that ATMI received PSL

data from Colonial months before ATMI’s testimony was due, and used that data to perform the

indicated corroborative calculations—is critical, because it shows that regardless of whether there

may be additional information in PSL’s possession that would further “corroborate” ATMI’s

hypothetical blend margins, ATMI was able to perform the calculations it claimed were necessary

using information provided to it in discovery by Colonial. ATMI’s speculation that “other”

information may have existed that it “could” have potentially used is just that—speculation. It is

certainly not evidence that Colonial engaged in wrongdoing or that ATMI suffered any harm.

            In addition, Colonial notes that virtually no party ever receives in discovery every shred of

information or data that it requests, nor is a party typically able to confirm that what it has received

is the universe of responsive material. But without more, that alone is insufficient to demonstrate

prejudice of any kind, much less undue prejudice that warrants imposing sanctions on the

responding party. Colonial notes that rather than a scheme to deceive ATMI, it was Colonial’s

open and honest acknowledgment that it did not know what, if any, additional responsive

information PSL possessed (beyond that already produced by Colonial) that led to ATMI’s claims

of harm and the Presiding Judge’s imposition of sanctions. Colonial submits that this manner of

honest disclosure in the context of discovery is not the type of behavior that should be discouraged

by the imposition of sanctions.




21
     ATMI Initial Brief at 12.
22
     Colonial Initial Brief at 9-12.

         Moreover, as discussed in the Colonial Initial Brief, 23 Mr. Hollerbach’s supplemental

rebuttal testimony suggests that the “other” PSL information that ATMI complains it did not

receive were copies of invoices, particularly butane and transportation invoices. This is another

critical point, as ATMI never requested such invoices in its data requests directed to Colonial that

initiated this dispute. 24 ATMI did seek copies of such invoices from ONEOK via the subpoenas. 25

Colonial cannot be sanctioned for a third party’s failure to produce information that was never

requested from Colonial. 26

         Finally, the ATMI Initial Brief acknowledges that Colonial did not challenge the PSL data

that Mr. Hollerbach used to develop his corroborative analysis (either at hearing or in post-hearing

initial brief), 27 further demonstrating that ATMI had no real need for the missing information that

it now relies upon to argue that the Presiding Judge should not only maintain, but increase, the

monetary sanctions that he recommended be imposed on Colonial. While Colonial does not

believe that Mr. Hollerbach’s analysis is relevant, Colonial acknowledged during oral argument

on the ATMI Motion for Sanctions that it would not and could not rely upon PSL data that had not

been produced to ATMI in an effort to undermine Mr. Hollerbach’s analysis. 28

         ATMI has also had multiple opportunities to specifically explain the information that it

allegedly did not receive and how not having that information impacted its case, yet it has chosen

not to do so. Instead, ATMI continues to offer nothing more than conclusory allegations that it

was harmed because there was “other” information it did not receive that possibly could have be

used as further “corroboration.” Such vague and unsupported assumptions do not justify the

imposition of any monetary sanctions against Colonial, much less an amount that is double that

the Presiding Judge’ recommended in the May 2026 Order and orders of magnitude more than the

Commission has ever imposed on any litigant in the Commission’s history.

        Commission precedent weighs against the imposition of sanctions in all but the “clearest

of cases.” 29 The facts of this case (as opposed to ATMI’s mischaracterizations) demonstrate that

this is anything but the “clearest of cases,” as ATMI has failed at every turn to provide any cohesive

explanation of what information it did not receive and why that information was necessary for

ATMI to make its case. Setting aside the issue of whether obtaining data for the sole purpose of

“corroboration” is actually necessary, this failure is particularly problematic for the Commission

here, where ATMI has confirmed that other data it did receive from Colonial in a timely fashion

was sufficient to perform the evaluation it believed was necessary for its case.

        B.      ATMI’s request that the Presiding Judge increase the monetary sanctions
                lacks merit.

        ATMI urges the Presiding Judge to increase the amount of the monetary sanctions that he

recommends Colonial be required to pay ATMI to $567,530, which is double the amount the

Presiding Judge recommended in the May 2026 Order, based on ATMI’s view of Colonial’s

participation in settlement discussions.30 Beyond the procedural reasons why ATMI’s argument




29
   Colonial Initial Brief at 19-20; Enron Power Mktg., 109 FERC ¶ 61,298, at P 10 (2004); Conn. Yankee Atomic
Power Co., 81 FERC ¶ 63,006, at 65,037-38 (1997).
30

should be rejected, as discussed further in Section II.C, there is also no factual support for ATMI’s

requested increase in sanctions.

        First, ATMI argues that even if ONEOK was to blame for some of the discovery delay,

ONEOK’s actions should be held against Colonial, not ATMI. 31 As support, ATMI refers to

Paragraph 39 of the May 2026 Order, where the Presiding Judge referred to five email

communications between ONEOK and Colonial that he concluded demonstrated a “joint effort to

manage ATMI’s access to the Powder Springs information rather than a good faith attempt by

Colonial to obtain and produce it.” 32 As discussed in the Colonial Initial Brief, there is no fair

reading of those email communications that even remotely suggests a collaborative attempt to

shield the PSL data from production. 33

        Specifically, four of the five emails referred to in Paragraph 39 of the May 2026 Order are

part of a single email thread between Colonial’s in-house counsel and ONEOK’s in-house counsel,

in which (1) Colonial notified ONEOK that a subpoena was going to be issued to PSL, (2) Colonial

indicated that, based on some recent discovery requests it had received, the subpoena might seek

information beyond that ATMI initially requested from Colonial, (3) ONEOK sought (and

Colonial provided) a copy of the protective order issued in this proceeding and (4) ONEOK sought

(and Colonial agreed to provide) a list of the counsel of record in this proceeding for conflicts

purposes. 34 None of these emails discuss any of the data or documents sought by ATMI, or even

remotely suggests a “joint effort” to shield that material from discovery. Colonial understands the

May 2026 Order concluded otherwise, but a reasonable reading of these emails reflects nothing

more than standard communications between two joint venture partners. These emails also do not

undermine Colonial’s position that the information ATMI was seeking via its third-party

subpoenas on ONEOK were above and beyond the financial information that ONEOK shares with

Colonial in the ordinary course of business in accordance with the PSL governing agreements.

         Second, ATMI argues the fact that it did not issue a formal request for the PSL governing

agreements to Colonial until November 2025 is not a reason to reduce the monetary sanctions

awarded to ATMI as compensation for fees incurred. 35 Specifically, ATMI claims that had it

requested the agreements earlier, Colonial likely would have objected to producing them, “as it

did with respect to every request for Powder Springs information,” and that the objection would

have “necessitated the required meet and confer process, a motion to compel and answer, oral

argument and the perfunctory interlocutory appeal.” 36 This argument ignores the fact that Colonial

is not obligated to respond to informal discovery requests—a fact that the Presiding Judge made

abundantly clear in a prior discovery order. 37 Further, ATMI’s claim that Colonial would have

fought the production of the PSL agreements through a motion to compel and interlocutory appeal

is undermined by the fact that Colonial did not do so when ATMI ultimately issued a formal data

request seeking those materials. Colonial did object to the production of such agreements on the

grounds of relevance, as is Colonial’s right (and as Colonial must do in order to preserve that

relevance objection at hearing), but Colonial ultimately produced the agreements without a motion

to compel or the so-called “perfunctory” interlocutory appeal.

         In truth, if any party has suffered “undue” prejudice and harm as a result of this issue, it

has been Colonial. Rather than preparing for the evidentiary hearing, Colonial was required to

devote its attention and resources to defending itself against ATMI’s claims that have been shown

to be baseless. In fact, the record supports that ATMI never truly needed or wanted the PSL data;

indeed, ATMI already had all of the PSL data it needed to perform the analysis it sought to perform

and, according to ONEOK’s counsel, ATMI appeared more interested in pursuing sanctions

against Colonial than it was in actually obtaining the additional requested PSL data that is the

center of this dispute. 38 Colonial has incurred hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal expenses

in order to defend itself from ATMI’s attacks and demonstrate that ATMI suffered no undue

prejudice from Colonial’s actions. The ATMI Initial Brief effectively admits this to be true.

Therefore, Colonial submits that the Presiding Judge should modify his recommendation and find

that no monetary sanctions are appropriate here, because it has been demonstrated that ATMI

suffered no undue prejudice.

         C.       Settlement negotiations cannot be used as evidence to prove the validity of a
                  claim.

         The ATMI Initial Brief extensively criticizes Colonial’s efforts to settle this issue, going

so far as to claim that Colonial participated in those negotiations in bad faith. 39 There is no merit

to these accusations, and in fact, it is this type of inflammatory and unsupported rhetoric—which

has become commonplace in ATMI’s pleadings—that led to the Presiding Judge’s erroneous

sanctions recommendation in the first place. Notably, the specter of attorney misconduct and

ethical sanctions was initially raised by ATMI only in a footnote, and it was clear from that

Nos. OR22-5-001 et al., at 2 (filed Feb. 23, 2026).

pleading that ATMI was seeking certain evidentiary sanctions, not monetary or ethical sanctions. 40

However, once the Presiding Judge showed interest in non-evidentiary sanctions, ATMI has been

forced to focus its subsequent discussions on monetary sanctions. Nevertheless, as discussed in

Section II.D below, Colonial at all times made good faith settlement overtures, while ATMI nearly

ended the settlement discussions before they meaningfully began by making a first offer [BEGIN

CUI//PRIV/HC]                                      [END CUI//PRIV/HC] recommended in the May

2026 Order. The fact that the settlement process was ultimately unsuccessful and that ATMI is

not happy with Colonial’s settlement offer does not demonstrate bad faith or any wrongdoing on

the part of Colonial.

           That aside, ATMI’s claims that Colonial’s behavior during those settlement discussions

provides the Presiding Judge with further evidence demonstrating that monetary sanctions are

appropriate are groundless. While Colonial acknowledges that the Presiding Judge stated that he

would consider the parties’ efforts at settlement, the nature and extent of those efforts is irrelevant

to the merits of the underlying issue.

           As an initial matter, Section 343.5 41 of the Commission’s regulations (cited in the July 17

Order) is not applicable in these circumstances. That regulation applies when the “Commission

or other decisional authority” requires the parties to “enter into good faith negotiations to settle oil

pipeline rate matters.” In this instance, the Commission has not required Colonial and ATMI to

enter settlement negotiations on this issue, and no settlement judge has been appointed to oversee

such negotiations (despite Colonial’s interest in obtaining such an appointment).

           The Commission’s approach of protecting the confidentiality of settlement discussions is

consistent with Federal Rules of Evidence Rule 408, which prohibits the use of settlement offers


40
     ATMI Motion for Sanctions at 25 n.42.
41
     18 C.F.R. § 343.5 (2026) (“Section 343.5”).

and negotiations in establishing the merits of any issue. 42 While the Federal Rules of Evidence

are not binding in FERC proceedings, as the Presiding Judge has previously recognized, they are

commonly recognized as persuasive authority on the appropriate interpretation of FERC’s own

rules, and as providing guidance where FERC’s rules are silent. 43 In this case, where a party has

actively participated in settlement negotiations and has in fact made an offer of settlement (as

discussed in more detail below), attempting to parse the details of those negotiations, assign blame

for the failure to settle, and then relying on that assessment of blame to make a ruling on the merits

of the issue is directly contrary to the guidance provided by the Federal Rules of Evidence, and is

antithetical to the Commission’s policy of ensuring the confidentiality of settlement discussions

and promoting settlement.

        Furthermore, in the Order on Certified Question, the Commission did not suggest that it

intended to rely on any settlement discussions to rule on the merits of this dispute; rather, the

Commission’s order indicated only that if a settlement was reached, the parties should address how

that settlement impacted the issue of sanctions. 44 The fact that settlement negotiations took place

is not confidential, but ATMI’s reliance on the settlement communications to support the merits

of its claim that Colonial should be subjected to monetary sanctions is untenable. For these

reasons, the Presiding Judge should not use the substance of settlement negotiations as evidence

in determining whether monetary sanctions are appropriate or the amount of appropriate monetary

sanctions.

           D.       Colonial participated in the settlement negotiations in good faith.

           Setting aside the fact that the settlement negotiations cannot be used in a determination on

the merits, Colonial categorically rejects ATMI’s characterizations of the settlement process and

submits that Colonial at all times participated in the settlement negotiations in good faith.

           While Colonial does not dispute that ATMI made the first settlement offer, that opening

offer was [BEGIN CUI//PRIV/HC]                                 [END CUI//PRIV/HC] the Presiding

Judge recommended in the May 2026 Order, strongly signaling to Colonial that settlement was

likely not feasible unless Colonial was willing simply to capitulate and accede to ATMI’s

demands. Rather than the starting point for settlement discussions being the amount recommended

by the Presiding Judge, as Colonial reasonably expected, ATMI demanded [BEGIN

CUI//PRIV/HC]




                [END CUI//PRIV/HC] and, as explained above, Colonial maintains that it engaged in
